en: Majjhima Nikāya 50:
Māratajjanīyasutta.
Thus have I heard—
On one occasion the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was dwelling among the Bhaggas at Susumāragira, in the Bhesakaḷā Grove, the Deer Park.
Now at that time, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was walking back and forth in the open air.
At that same time, Māra the Evil One had entered the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna’s belly, having gone inside his stomach.
Then it occurred to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna:
"Why is it that my belly feels so heavy,
as if it were filled with months?"
Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, having descended from his walking path and entered the dwelling, sat down on the prepared seat.
Having sat down, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna applied systematic attention within himself.
He saw Māra the Evil One, who had entered his belly and gone into his stomach.
Having seen him, he said this to Māra the Evil One:
“Depart, Evil One!
Depart, Evil One!”
"Do not harass the Tathāgata; do not harass the disciple of the Tathāgata.
Let it not lead to your own harm and suffering for a long time.
Then, this thought occurred to Māra the Evil One:
“Not knowing me at all and not seeing me, this ascetic said to me:
‘Come out, Evil One!
Come out, Evil One!’”
"Do not harass the Tathāgata; do not harass the disciple of the Tathāgata.
Let it not lead to your harm and suffering for a long time.
"Even that teacher of mine would not have known me quickly; how then could this disciple know me?"
Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said this to Māra the Evil One:
“Even thus do I know you, Evil One; do not think:
‘He does not know me.’”
"You are Māra, O Evil One!
For it occurs to you thus, O Evil One:
'This ascetic speaks thus to me while not knowing me and not seeing me.'"
Depart, O Evil One;
depart, O Evil One.
Do not harass the Tathāgata, nor the disciple of the Tathāgata.
"May this not lead to your harm and suffering for a long time!
Even that teacher of yours would not have known me quickly; how much less could this disciple know me?
Then it occurred to Māra the Evil One:
“Clearly this ascetic knows me as he looks at me when he says:
‘Come out, Evil One!
Come out, Evil One!’”
"Do not harass the Tathāgata; do not harass the disciple of the Tathāgata.
Let it not lead to your harm and suffering for a long time.
Then Māra the Evil One, having emerged from the mouth of the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, stood against the door-post.
The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna saw Māra the Evil One standing at the threshold;
having seen him, he said this to Māra the Evil One:
"I see you here too, Evil One! Do not think thus."
‘He does not see me.
You, Evil One, stand right against the door-post.
Once upon a time, Evil One, I was a Māra named Dūsī, and I had a sister named Kāḷī.
You were her son;
you were my nephew at that time.
Furthermore, Pāpima, at that time the Blessed One Kakusandha, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One, had appeared in the world.
Moreover, Pāpima, the Blessed One Kakusandha, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, had a pair of chief disciples named Vidhura and Sañjīva, a most auspicious pair.
And among all the disciples of the Blessed One Kakusandha, O Pāpima,
there was none who was the equal of the Venerable Vidhura in this regard, namely, in the teaching of the Dhamma.
It was by this very method, Evil One, that the venerable Vidhura’s designation as ‘Vidhura’ arose.
But the venerable Sañjīva, Evil One, whether he has gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, enters the cessation of perception and feeling with ease.
Once in the past, Evil One, the venerable Sañjīva was sitting at the foot of a certain tree, having entered the cessation of perception and feeling.
“Māra, the evil one, cowherds, shepherds, farmers, and travelers saw the Venerable Sañjīva sitting at the foot of a certain tree, having attained the cessation of perception and feeling.
Upon seeing him, it occurred to them:
‘How wonderful, indeed! How marvelous, indeed!’”
“This ascetic has passed away even while sitting;
come, let us cremate him.
Then, Evil One, those cowherds, shepherds, farmers, and travelers gathered grass, wood, and cow dung, piled it over the body of the Venerable Sañjīva, set fire to it, and departed.

Then, Evil One, at the end of that night, the Venerable Sañjīva emerged from that meditative attainment. He shook out his robes, dressed for the morning, and taking his bowl and outer robe, entered the village for alms.
While he was walking for alms, Evil One, those cowherds, shepherds, farmers, and travelers saw the Venerable Sañjīva;
having seen him, they thought to themselves:
“It is wonderful, indeed, sir! It is marvelous, indeed, sir!
This ascetic has passed away while still sitting, yet he has been restored to life!
By this means, Evil One, the designation “Sañjīva” (the Reviver) arose for the Venerable Sañjīva.
Then, Evil One, it occurred to Māra Dūsī:
"I do not know the coming or the going of these bhikkhus who are virtuous and of beautiful character.
Suppose I were to possess the brahmins and householders?"
"Come now, monks, revile, abuse, provoke, and harass those bhikkhus who are virtuous and of good character.
Perhaps, while being reviled, abused, provoked, and harassed by you, there might be some change of heart in them, whereby Māra Dūsī might find an opportunity.
Then, Evil One, Māra Dūsī possessed those brahmins and householders.
"Come now, you should revile, abuse, irritate, and harass those monks who are virtuous and of good character.
Perhaps, being thus reviled, abused, irritated, and harassed by you, there might be some change of heart in them, whereby Māra Dūsī might find an opportunity.
Then, O Evil One, those brahmins and householders, possessed by Māra Dūsī, reviled, abused, irritated, and harassed those monks who were virtuous and of good character.

"But these shaveling ascetics, these outcasts, these dark fellows, descendants of Bandhupādā, claim: 'We are meditators, we are meditators! and with shoulders drooping and heads downcast, they meditate, premeditate, postmeditate, and mismeditate with a sweet expression on their faces.
They are just like an owl perched on a tree branch, meditating, premeditating, postmeditating, and mismeditating while hunting for a mouse."

In the same way, these shavelings, these wretched recluses, these outcasts, these dark fellows who are the descendants of the slave Bandhula, thinking “we are meditators, we are meditators,” sit with shoulders hunched and heads cast down,

muttering sweet-sounding words as they meditate, premeditate, postmeditate, and mismeditate— just like a jackal on a riverbank, meditating, premeditating, postmeditating, and mismeditating while hunting for fish.

In the same way, these shavelings, these wretched little ascetics, these menials, dark fellows, the descendants of Bandhupādā, thinking “we are meditators, we are meditators,” with shoulders hunched and heads bowed,

muttering sweetly, meditate, premeditate, postmeditate, and mismeditate— just as a cat at a door-jamb, in a dusty corner, meditates, premeditates, postmeditates, and mismeditates while stalking a mouse.

In the same way, these shavelings, these wretched ascetics, these outcasts, the dark descendants of Bandhupadāpaccā, thinking “we are meditators, we are meditators,” sit with shoulders hunched and heads bowed, muttering sweetly as they meditate, premeditate, postmeditate,
and mismeditate— just like a donkey, when its load is removed, sits, premeditates, postmeditates, and mismeditates upon a muddy, slippery, and narrow embankment.

"In the same way, these shavelings, these wretched recluses, these outcasts, these dark fellows who are descendants of Bandhupādāpacca, thinking 'we are meditators, we are meditators,' sit with shoulders hunched and heads bowed, muttering sweetly as they meditate, premeditate, postmeditate, and mismeditate.
And at that time, Pāpima, most of those people who died were, upon the breakup of the body after death, reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell.
Then, Pāpima, the Blessed One Kakusandha, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One, addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, the brahmin householders have been possessed by Māra the Corrupter:
‘Come now, revile, abuse, irritate, and harass the bhikkhus who are virtuous and of good character;
perhaps, while being reviled, abused, irritated, and harassed by you, they might [fall away].’”
“Otherwise there might be a change of mind, so that Māra the Corrupter might find an opportunity.
“Come, monks, dwell pervading one quarter with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth;
thus above, below, across, everywhere, and to all as to yourselves.”
Dwell pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness—vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will.
[Dwell] with a mind imbued with compassion... [and so on].
Abide pervading one quarter with a mind imbued with sympathetic joy …pe… with a mind imbued with equanimity; likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth.
Thus above, below, across, everywhere, and to all as to yourself, abide pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with equanimity.
‘Dwell pervading with a mind that is vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity,
and free from ill will. Then, Evil One, those bhikkhus, being thus exhorted and thus instructed by the Blessed One Kakusandha, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One,
whether gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, dwelt with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness.
They dwelt pervading one quarter with a mind imbued with loving-kindness; likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth.

Thus, above, below, across, and everywhere, to all as to themselves, they dwelt pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness—vast, exalted, measureless, free from enmity, and free from ill will.
With a mind imbued with compassion …pe… with a mind imbued with sympathetic joy …pe… with a mind imbued with equanimity,
they dwelt pervading one direction, likewise the second, likewise the third, [and the fourth].

And so it was with the fourth. Thus, above, below, across, and everywhere, in all respects, they dwelt pervading the entire world with a mind accompanied by equanimity—vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will.
Then, Evil One, it occurred to Dūsi Māra:
‘Even though I am acting in this way, I still do not know the coming or the going of these virtuous monks of beautiful character. What if I were to influence the brahmins and householders, saying:
“Come, you should honor, revere, respect, and worship these virtuous monks of beautiful character;
perhaps, while they are being honored, revered, respected, and worshipped by you, there might be some change in their minds, so that the Māra Dūsī might find an opportunity?”’”
Then, Evil One, Dūsī Māra possessed those brahmins and householders:
“Come now, you should honor, revere, respect, and worship those monks who are virtuous and of good character;
perhaps, while they are being honored, revered, respected, and worshipped by you, there might be some change in their minds, whereby Dūsī Māra might find an opportunity.”
Then, Evil One, those brahmin householders, being possessed by the corrupting Māra, honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped the monks who were virtuous and of good character.
And at that time, Evil One, most of those people who died passed away from the breaking up of the body after death and were reborn in a happy destination, a heavenly world.
Then, Evil One, the Blessed One Kakusandha, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, addressed the monks:
“Bhikkhus, the brahmin householders have been possessed by the corrupting Māra, who says:
‘Come now, you should honor, respect, revere, and venerate those bhikkhus who are virtuous and of good character;
perhaps, while they are being honored, respected, revered, and venerated by you, there might be some alteration in their minds, whereby the corrupting Māra might find an opportunity.’”

"Come, monks, dwell contemplating the foulness in the body, perceiving the repulsiveness in food, perceiving non-delight in the entire world, and contemplating impermanence in all conditioned phenomena. Then, O Evil One, those monks,

being thus exhorted and thus instructed by the Blessed One Kakusandha, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, went to the forest, to the foot of trees, or to empty huts, dwelling there contemplating the foulness in the body.
They dwelt perceiving the body as such, perceiving repulsiveness in food, perceiving non-delight in the entire world, and contemplating impermanence in all conditioned phenomena.

Then, Pāpima, in the morning, the Blessed One Kakusandha, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, dressed himself, took his bowl and robe, and entered the village for alms with the Venerable Vidhura as his attendant monk.
Then, Pāpima, Māra Dūsī possessed a certain young boy, who took a pebble and struck the Venerable Vidhura on the head, splitting his skull.
Then, Evil One, with his head split open and blood flowing, the venerable Vidhura followed closely behind the Blessed One Kakusandha, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Then, Evil One, the Blessed One Kakusandha, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, looked back with the gaze of an elephant, thinking:
"This Māra Dūsī has not yet had enough."
And because he looked on with indifference, O Evil One, Dūsī Māra fell from that place and was reborn in the Great Niraya hell.
Now, Evil One, that Great Niraya hell has three names:
it is called "The Six Bases of Contact," it is called "The Pierced by Arrows," and it is also called "To Be Experienced Individually."
Then, Evil One, the wardens of hell approached me and said this:
“When, dear sir, spike meets spike in your heart,
then you will know it.”
“For a thousand years I was being cooked in hell,” he said.
And so, Evil One, for many years, many hundreds of years, and many thousands of years I was cooked in that great hell.
For ten thousand years I was cooked in the *ussada* (supplementary) sections of that very same great hell, experiencing the sensation called *vuṭṭhānima*.
“Māra, my body was such as that of a human being;
my head was such as that of a fish. What was that hell like?”
Where Dūsi was roasted,
having assailed his disciple Vidhura and the brahmin Kakusandha.
There were hundreds of iron spikes,
each one a personal sensation of suffering;
such was that hell.
Where Dūsi was roasted,
having assailed his disciple Vidhura and the brahmin Kakusandha.
The monk who assails such a bhikkhu— a disciple of the Buddha who has direct knowledge of this— [is lost].
O Kaṇha, you shall undergo suffering.
In the midst of the lake stand celestial mansions that endure for an eon.
Lustrous, with the color of beryl,
radiant and glowing,
celestial nymphs dance there.
Diverse and of various appearances.
The bhikkhu who is a disciple of the Buddha thoroughly understands this;
Having assailed such a bhikkhu,
O Kaṇha, you shall undergo suffering.
For he who has been reproved by the Buddha—
While the Saṅgha was looking on,
the bhikkhu made the Migāramātupāsāda tremble with his big toe.
Whosoever, a bhikkhu who is a disciple of the Buddha,
assails such a bhikkhu as this—
O Kaṇha, you shall undergo suffering,
you who indeed caused the Vejayanta Palace to tremble with your big toe.
Firmly established in the power of psychic success,
he inspired awe in the deities;
whoever understands this—
A monk is a disciple of the Buddha;
by assailing such a monk,
O Dark One, you shall undergo suffering.

He who, in the Vejayanta Palace, questioned Sakka: "Do you know, Vāsava, "Is there anyone else besides me who knows this Dhamma?"—it was he who asked this question. 1605. The Blessed One, knowing his inclination, taught him the Dhamma that leads to liberation. Having heard it, he attained the fruit of stream-entry. 1606. Then, having attained the fruit, he spoke thus to the Teacher: "I have understood the Dhamma; I am one who has reached the goal. 1607. The Teacher, knowing his attainment, said: "Welcome, bhikkhu. He then ordained him with the formal act of the threefold repetition. 1608. Having been ordained, he dwelt in the forest, practicing meditation. By means of diligent effort, he realized the state of an arahant. 1609. Having become an arahant, he went to the Teacher and spoke: "I have crossed over the ocean of existence; I have reached the further shore. I am now free from all suffering. 1610. The Teacher, knowing his realization, praised him: "Well done, bhikkhu! You have indeed accomplished what was difficult to do. 1611. Thus did the Elder Sela, having attained the supreme state, live in peace, having fulfilled his purpose. 1612. This is the story of the Elder Sela, who, through the power of the Buddha, attained the fruit of arahantship. 1613. May this merit bring peace and happiness to all beings. May they all cross over the great ocean of saṃsāra. 1614. May the Dhamma shine brightly for a long time. May the Saṅgha flourish and prosper. 1615. May all beings be free from fear and sorrow. May they dwell in harmony and peace. 1616. Thus ends the narrative of the Elder Sela. It is a source of joy and inspiration for all who hear it. 1617. May this recital be auspicious. May it lead to the cessation of suffering for all. 1618. Thus have I heard: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in the Jeta Grove, the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍika. 1619. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: "Bhikkhus! "Venerable sir," they replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then spoke as follows: 1620. "Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who goes from darkness to light; the person who goes from light to darkness; the person who goes from darkness to darkness; and the person who goes from light to light. 1621. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person who goes from darkness to light? Here, bhikkhus, a certain person is reborn in a low family—a family of outcasts, hunters, bamboo-workers, cartwrights, or scavengers—one that is poor, with little food and drink, lacking the necessities of life, where food and clothing are obtained with difficulty. 1622. And he is ugly, unsightly, and ill-favored, with limbs that are deformed, sickly, and afflicted by many diseases, such as blindness, deafness, lameness, or paralysis. 1623. Yet he possesses unwavering faith in the Buddha: 'The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Fortunate One. 1624. He also possesses unwavering faith in the Dhamma: 'The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. 1625. He also possesses unwavering faith in the Saṅgha: 'The Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals. This Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. 1626. But he does not fulfill the training in the higher virtue, nor does he fulfill the training in the higher mind, nor does he fulfill the training in the higher wisdom. 1627. However, by the destruction of the three fetters, he becomes a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower realms, fixed in destiny, and assured of enlightenment. This, bhikkhus, is called a person who goes from darkness to light. 1628. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person who goes from light to darkness? Here, bhikkhus, a certain person is reborn in a high family—a family of kshatriyas, brahmins, or householders—one that is rich, with abundant wealth and property, possessing vast assets and many resources, with a full treasury and granary. 1629. And he is handsome, attractive, and pleasing to behold, with limbs that are well-formed, healthy, and free from disease, not blind, not deaf, not lame, and not paralyzed. 1630. Yet he does not possess unwavering faith in the Buddha... [as in 1623] ...nor does he possess unwavering faith in the Dhamma... [as in 1624] ...nor does he possess unwavering faith in the Saṅgha... [as in 1625]. 1631. But he fulfills the training in the higher virtue, and he fulfills the training in the higher mind, and he fulfills the training in the higher wisdom. 1632. However, by the destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one of spontaneous birth, attaining nibbāna there without returning from that world. This, bhikkhus, is called a person who goes from light to darkness. 1633. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person who goes from darkness to darkness? Here, bhikkhus, a certain person is reborn in a low family... [as in 1621] ...and he is ugly, unsightly, and ill-favored... [as in 1622]. 1634. And he does not possess unwavering faith in the Buddha... [as in 1623] ...nor does he possess unwavering faith in the Dhamma... [as in 1624] ...nor does he possess unwavering faith in the Saṅgha... [as in 1625]. 1635.

And he does not fulfill the training in the higher virtue, nor does he fulfill the training in the higher mind, nor does he fulfill the training in the higher wisdom. 1636. And by the destruction of the three fetters, along with greed, hatred, and delusion, he becomes a once-returner, who returns to this world only once more and then makes an end of suffering. This, bhikkhus, is called a person who goes from darkness to darkness. 1637. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person who goes from light to light? Here, bhikkhus, a certain person is reborn in a high family... [as in 1628] ...and he is handsome, attractive, and pleasing to behold... [as in 1629]. 1638. And he possesses unwavering faith in the Buddha... [as in 1623] ...he possesses unwavering faith in the Dhamma... [as in 1624] ...and he possesses unwavering faith in the Saṅgha... [as in 1625]. 1639. And he fulfills the training in the higher virtue, and he fulfills the training in the higher mind, and he fulfills the training in the higher wisdom. 1640. And by the destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one of spontaneous birth, attaining nibbāna there without returning from that world. This, bhikkhus, is called a person who goes from light to light. 1641. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. 1642. When the Blessed One had spoken thus, the venerable Sela said to the Blessed One: "Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir! Just as if one were to set upright what had been overturned, or to reveal what was hidden, or to point out the way to one who was lost, or to bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms, even so has the Dhamma been made clear by the Blessed One in many ways. 1643. I go for refuge to the Blessed One, and to the
Regarding the liberation through the destruction of craving,
Sakka, being questioned, answered that question exactly as it is.
The monk who is a disciple of the Buddha understands this; having assailed such a monk,
[one would incur great harm].
O Kaṇha, you shall undergo suffering,
you who question the Brahmā in the assembly hall out of fear for the True Dhamma.
Even now, friend, you still hold that same view you held before;
do you see it passing away?
In the Brahma-world, it was radiant.
Brahmā explained it to him in due order, exactly as it is.
"O worthy sir, that view which I formerly held is no longer mine.
I see it passing away."
Radiant in the Brahma-world;
how could I say today,
"I am eternal and permanent"?
Whosoever, a bhikkhu who is a disciple of the Buddha,
assails such a bhikkhu as this—
O Kaṇha, you shall undergo suffering,
you who have touched the peak of Mount Mahāmeru with your liberation.
The forest of the Pubbavideha people and those men who dwell upon the earth—
he who fully understands this, [is a sage].
A bhikkhu is a disciple of the Buddha;
by assailing such a bhikkhu,
O Kaṇha, you undergo suffering.
The fire does not think,
"I am burning the fool";
yet the fool [is burned] by the blazing fire.
Having assailed him, he is consumed. Even so, O Māra,
having assailed the Tathāgata;
You will burn yourself,
O fool, like one who touches fire;
Māra has produced demerit.
Having assailed the Tathāgata, what do you think, O Evil One?
"Does my evil not ripen for me? [you ask].
Evil is heaped up for a long time, O End-maker;
O Māra, be weary of the Buddha.
"Do not harbor expectations among the bhikkhus.
Thus did he rebuke Māra in the Bhesakaḷā Grove, O bhikkhu.
Then that dejected yakkha vanished right there.
The tenth sutta, the Māratajjanīya Sutta, is finished.
The fifth chapter, the Cūḷayamaka-vagga, is finished.
Its summary verse (uddāna) is: Sāleyya, Verañja, Duvaka, and Tuṭṭhi.
The Cūḷa- and Mahā-dhammasamādāna,
the Vīmaṁsaka, Kosambī, and the Brāhmaṇa,
and Dūsī Māra as the tenth— this is the section.
This is the summary of the sections:
the Mūlapariyāya and the supreme Sīhanāda;
Kakaca, Gosiṅga, and Sāleyya—
these are the five.
The Root Fifty is completed.
